claims.text: Tensile strain at a transition-metal/support interface shifts the d-band center of the active metal sites.
A strain-induced d-band-center shift enhances adsorption of key reactant molecules.
Enhanced reactant adsorption caused by tensile strain increases catalytic activity.
Engineering lattice mismatch between a support and a metal catalyst can induce controlled tensile strain.
Holding temperature, pressure, and reactant concentrations constant isolates induced strain as the sole cause of observed performance differences.
Tensile strain shifts the d-band center closer to the Fermi level.
Moving the d-band center closer to the Fermi level lowers activation barriers for reactant adsorption.
Lower adsorption barriers produce enhanced reactant adsorption.
Enhanced reactant adsorption leads to increased catalytic activity.
Tensile-strained catalysts will have higher catalytic reaction rates than unstrained controls under identical reaction conditions.
Tensile-strained catalysts will exhibit improved adsorption characteristics relative to unstrained controls.
The proposed effect should hold when reaction kinetics are sensitive to adsorption and strain-induced electronic effects dominate activity modulation.
The proposed effect may not hold in systems dominated by mass-transport limitations.
The proposed effect may not hold when active-site chemistry is insensitive to electronic-structure variation.
No direct evidence is provided linking induced tensile strain to a d-band-center shift and improved activity.
Alternative interfacial effects or structural changes could contribute to any observed activity difference.
